claim: Eukaryotic histones wrap ~147 DNA base pairs into nucleosomes.
source: While the four eukaryotic histones wrap ~147 DNA base pairs into nucleosomes, archaeal histones form 'nucleosome-like' complexes that continuously wind between 60 and 500 base pairs of DNA ('archaeasomes'), suggested by crystal contacts and analysis of cellular chromatin.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of chromatin biology, supported by the citation to Luger et al., 1997 in the Introduction.

claim: Archaeal histones form 'nucleosome-like' complexes that continuously wind between 60 and 500 base pairs of DNA.
source: While the four eukaryotic histones wrap ~147 DNA base pairs into nucleosomes, archaeal histones form 'nucleosome-like' complexes that continuously wind between 60 and 500 base pairs of DNA ('archaeasomes'), suggested by crystal contacts and analysis of cellular chromatin.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystal contacts and analysis of cellular chromatin as stated in the text, and is further supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Solution structures of large archaeasomes (>90 DNA base pairs) have never been directly observed prior to this study.
source: Solution structures of large archaeasomes (>90 DNA base pairs) have never been directly observed.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to the current work, establishing the novelty of the study.

claim: Simulations reveal dynamics of increased accessibility without disruption of DNA-binding or tetramerization interfaces in archaeasomes.
source: Simulations reveal dynamics of increased accessibility without disruption of DNA-binding or tetramerization interfaces.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the molecular dynamics simulations presented in the Results section.

claim: Mg2+ concentration influences archaeasome compaction.
source: Mg2+ concentration influences compaction, and cryoEM densities illustrate that DNA is wrapped in consecutive substates arranged 90o out-of-plane with one another.
evidence: This is supported by SV-AUC data showing changes in sedimentation and frictional ratio with varying Mg2+ concentrations.

claim: CryoEM densities illustrate that DNA is wrapped in consecutive substates arranged 90° out-of-plane with one another in archaeasomes.
source: Mg2+ concentration influences compaction, and cryoEM densities illustrate that DNA is wrapped in consecutive substates arranged 90o out-of-plane with one another.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryoEM structures presented in the Results section.

claim: Archaea may leverage inherent archaeasome dynamics to balance chromatin packing and accessibility without ATP-dependent remodelers.
source: Without ATP-dependent remodelers, archaea may leverage these inherent dynamics to balance chromatin packing and accessibility.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed dynamics and the apparent absence of ATP-dependent remodelers in archaea.

claim: Eukaryotic genomes are orders of magnitude larger and more complex than those of archaea or bacteria.
source: Eukaryotic genomes are orders of magnitude larger and more complex than those of archaea or bacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge in genomics and cell biology.

claim: Eukaryotic nucleosomes contain two H2A-H2B histone heterodimers flanking a central (H3-H4)2 heterotetramer and stably wrap ~147 base pairs of DNA.
source: They manage their massive genomes through a hierarchical packaging scheme that utilizes histones to form nucleosomes, a complex that contains two H2A-H2B histone heterodimers flanking a central (H3-H4)2 heterotetramer and stably wraps ~147 base pairs of DNA (Figure 1A; Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Luger et al., 1997 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: All eukaryotes invariably contain histones.
source: While all eukaryotes invariably contain histones, genes encoding putative 'minimalist' histone proteins have been identified in most archaea (Henneman et al., 2018), but so far not in bacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Genes encoding putative 'minimalist' histone proteins have been identified in most archaea.
source: While all eukaryotes invariably contain histones, genes encoding putative 'minimalist' histone proteins have been identified in most archaea (Henneman et al., 2018), but so far not in bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Henneman et al., 2018.

claim: Histone genes have not been identified in bacteria so far.
source: While all eukaryotes invariably contain histones, genes encoding putative 'minimalist' histone proteins have been identified in most archaea (Henneman et al., 2018), but so far not in bacteria.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The presence of histones in eukaryotes and archaea has supported theories that eukaryotes evolved directly from an archaeon.
source: While still a subject of debate, the presence of histones in the two domains of life has supported theories that eukaryotes evolved directly from an archaeon (Heinicke et al., 2004; Malik and Henikoff, 2003; Brunk and Martin, 2019; Watson, 2019; Eme et al., 2017; Spang et al., 2018; Sandman and Reeve, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to evolutionary biology literature.

claim: Archaeal histones share the three-helix histone fold motif (α1-L1-α2-L2-α3) with eukaryotic histones.
source: Archaeal histones share many features with their eukaryotic equivalents, such as the three-helix histone fold motif (α1-L1-α2-L2-α3) (Decanniere et al., 2000), as well as obligate dimerization and transient tetramer formation (Marc et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Decanniere et al., 2000.

claim: Archaeal histones exhibit obligate dimerization and transient tetramer formation.
source: Archaeal histones share many features with their eukaryotic equivalents, such as the three-helix histone fold motif (α1-L1-α2-L2-α3) (Decanniere et al., 2000), as well as obligate dimerization and transient tetramer formation (Marc et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Marc et al., 2002.

claim: In both archaea and eukaryotes, histones have a preference for occupying particular sites in the genome.
source: In both archaea and eukaryotes, histones have a preference for occupying particular sites in the genome (Ammar et al., 2012; Nalabothula et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ammar et al., 2012 and Nalabothula et al., 2013.

claim: Eukaryotic histones utilize highly disordered cationic N-terminal tails to regulate gene transcription and chromosome compaction via post-translational modifications.
source: Eukaryotic histones utilize highly disordered cationic N-terminal tails to regulate gene transcription and chromosome compaction via post-translational modifications (PTMs) (Luger and Richmond, 1998; Musselman et al., 2012; Bowman and Poirier, 2015), whereas most archaeal histones do not contain tail sequences, with the exception of some sequences found within the Asgard clade (Henneman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature on histone modifications.

claim: Most archaeal histones do not contain tail sequences, with the exception of some sequences found within the Asgard clade.
source: Eukaryotic histones utilize highly disordered cationic N-terminal tails to regulate gene transcription and chromosome compaction via post-translational modifications (PTMs) (Luger and Richmond, 1998; Musselman et al., 2012; Bowman and Poirier, 2015), whereas most archaeal histones do not contain tail sequences, with the exception of some sequences found within the Asgard clade (Henneman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Henneman et al., 2018.

claim: Eukaryotic histones have evolved histone fold 'extensions', unique secondary structure elements that define the outer surface of the nucleosome and stabilize the histone core and the final turn of nucleosomal DNA.
source: Additionally, histones in eukaryotes have evolved histone fold 'extensions', unique secondary structure elements that define the outer surface of the nucleosome as well as stabilize the histone core and the final turn of nucleosomal DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nucleosome structure.

claim: No histone fold extensions have been identified in any of the archaeal histones.
source: No such diversification has yet been identified in any of the archaeal histones.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding archaeal histone structure.

claim: The crystal structure of Methanothermus fervidus histone HMfB bound to ~90 base pairs of DNA was determined.
source: Recently, we determined the crystal structure of Methanothermus fervidus histone HMfB bound to ~90 base pairs of DNA (Mattiroli et al., 2017; Bhattacharyya et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mattiroli et al., 2017 and Bhattacharyya et al., 2018.

claim: HMfB is a typical representative of most archaeal histones, containing no tails and no histone fold extensions.
source: HMfB is a typical representative of most archaeal histones, as it contains no tails and no histone fold extensions, and it exists as either a homodimer or heterodimer with the closely related HMfA histone (Sandman et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Sandman et al., 1994.

claim: HMfB exists as either a homodimer or heterodimer with the closely related HMfA histone.
source: HMfB is a typical representative of most archaeal histones, as it contains no tails and no histone fold extensions, and it exists as either a homodimer or heterodimer with the closely related HMfA histone (Sandman et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Sandman et al., 1994.

claim: The HMfB-DNA crystal structure shows striking similarities to the eukaryotic nucleosome, including a superhelical DNA path around a histone core nearly identical to that in nucleosomes.
source: Nevertheless, striking similarities to the eukaryotic nucleosome were observed, including a superhelical DNA path around a histone core that is nearly identical to that in nucleosomes, promoted by conserved DNA contacts with histones, and by dimer-dimer interactions through 'four-helix bundles' of α-helices.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: Crystal contacts in the archaeal histone-DNA system promote an extended superhelical winding of DNA around a histone core consisting of more than the canonical four histone dimers.
source: However, unlike nucleosomes, which are defined octameric particles that arrange as 10 nm 'beads on a string' on long DNA fragments, crystal contacts in the archaeal system promote an extended superhelical winding of DNA around a histone core that consists of more than the canonical four histone dimers.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The crystal structure arrangement is consistent with in vivo footprinting results.
source: This arrangement, which is consistent with in vivo footprinting results (Mattiroli et al., 2017), places the L1 loops of every nth and (n+3)th dimer in close proximity to one another (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Mattiroli et al., 2017.

claim: The L1-L1 interaction is important in stabilizing the archaeasome arrangement in vitro and in vivo.
source: The importance of the L1-L1 interaction in stabilizing this arrangement in vitro and in vivo was established by substituting the highly conserved G17 residue with bulkier amino acids (e.g. G17D), resulting in transcription regulation defects.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: Substituting the highly conserved G17 residue with bulkier amino acids (e.g. G17D) results in transcription regulation defects.
source: The importance of the L1-L1 interaction in stabilizing this arrangement in vitro and in vivo was established by substituting the highly conserved G17 residue with bulkier amino acids (e.g. G17D), resulting in transcription regulation defects.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: Archaeal histones, when assembled on long segments of DNA (>200 base pairs), experience disparate solution dynamics compared to eukaryotic nucleosomes.
source: Here, we show that archaeal histones, when assembled on long segments of DNA (>200 base pairs), experience disparate solution dynamics compared to eukaryotic nucleosomes, and we present cryo-EM structures of two classes of particles arranged on a 207 base pair DNA fragment with deflections of the wrapping pathway.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on MD simulations, SV-AUC, and cryoEM data.

claim: Two classes of archaeasome particles arranged on a 207 base pair DNA fragment show deflections of the wrapping pathway.
source: Here, we show that archaeal histones, when assembled on long segments of DNA (>200 base pairs), experience disparate solution dynamics compared to eukaryotic nucleosomes, and we present cryo-EM structures of two classes of particles arranged on a 207 base pair DNA fragment with deflections of the wrapping pathway.
evidence: This is based on cryoEM structural data presented in the Results section.

claim: Archaeasomes can expand, like the stretching of a 'slinky', to increase overall accessibility without sacrificing histone-histone or histone-DNA interactions.
source: We use molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to show that archaeasomes can expand, like the stretching of a 'slinky', to increase overall accessibility without sacrificing histone-histone or histone-DNA interactions.
evidence: This is based on MD simulation data presented in the Results section.

claim: L1-L1 histone stacking interactions regulate the dynamic equilibrium of archaeasomes.
source: Simulations also reinforce the importance of L1-L1 histone stacking interactions in regulating this dynamic equilibrium.
evidence: This is based on MD simulation data comparing wild-type and G17D mutant systems.

claim: SV-AUC and cryoEM highlight two distinct accessibility dynamics at play in archaeasome systems.
source: Sedimentation velocity analytical ultracentrifugation (SV-AUC) and cryoEM highlight two distinct accessibility dynamics at play in archaeasome systems, and cryoEM analysis identifies archaeasomal states that continually wrap DNA but deflect the wrapping pathway 90o out-of-plane.
evidence: This is based on SV-AUC and cryoEM data presented in the Results section.

claim: CryoEM analysis identifies archaeasomal states that continually wrap DNA but deflect the wrapping pathway 90° out-of-plane.
source: Sedimentation velocity analytical ultracentrifugation (SV-AUC) and cryoEM highlight two distinct accessibility dynamics at play in archaeasome systems, and cryoEM analysis identifies archaeasomal states that continually wrap DNA but deflect the wrapping pathway 90o out-of-plane.
evidence: This is based on cryoEM structural data presented in the Results section.

claim: The intrinsic dynamic behavior of archaeasome slinkies stands in contrast to eukaryotic nucleosomes, which are compact and highly stable.
source: The intrinsic dynamic behavior of archaeasome slinkies stands in contrast to eukaryotic nucleosomes, which are compact and highly stable and require modifications and elaborate machinery to efficiently regulate chromatin accessibility, whereas archaea may utilize this inherent stochastic behavior in order to access their DNA.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the archaeasome data with known properties of eukaryotic nucleosomes.

claim: Eukaryotic nucleosomes require modifications and elaborate machinery to efficiently regulate chromatin accessibility.
source: The intrinsic dynamic behavior of archaeasome slinkies stands in contrast to eukaryotic nucleosomes, which are compact and highly stable and require modifications and elaborate machinery to efficiently regulate chromatin accessibility, whereas archaea may utilize this inherent stochastic behavior in order to access their DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic chromatin regulation.

claim: In each simulated archaeasome system, the DNA footprint of ~30 base pairs per dimer was maintained on the hundreds of nanoseconds timescale.
source: In each system, the DNA footprint of ~30 base pairs per dimer was maintained on the hundreds of nanoseconds timescale.
evidence: This is based on analysis of MD simulation trajectories.

claim: The Arc90 system experienced a high degree of global dynamics with a maximum RMSD deviation of ~6 Å from the initial coordinates.
source: Nevertheless, the Arc90 system experienced a high degree of global dynamics. RMSD calculations of backbone atom positions showed a maximum deviation of ~6 Å from the initial Arc90 coordinates, with trough-to-peak heights of ~4 Å throughout the time course (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on RMSD calculations from MD simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: RMSF calculations identify regions of highest flexibility where the DNA binds to the terminal dimers in Arc90.
source: RMSF calculations identify regions of highest flexibility where the DNA binds to the terminal dimers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and visual inspection of Arc90 trajectories revealed that the system samples a 'clamshell' motion, where terminal dimers and associated DNA fluctuate to create 'closed' and 'open' accessibility states (Videos 4 and 5).
evidence: This is based on RMSF analysis of MD simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Arc90 trajectories show that the system samples a 'clamshell' motion, where terminal dimers and associated DNA fluctuate to create 'closed' and 'open' accessibility states.
source: RMSF calculations identify regions of highest flexibility where the DNA binds to the terminal dimers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and visual inspection of Arc90 trajectories revealed that the system samples a 'clamshell' motion, where terminal dimers and associated DNA fluctuate to create 'closed' and 'open' accessibility states (Videos 4 and 5).
evidence: This is based on visual inspection of MD simulation trajectories shown in Videos 4 and 5.

claim: Over the clamshell motion in Arc90, the four-helix bundle interfaces that bind consecutive dimers to one another were maintained.
source: Over the clamshell motion, the four-helix bundle interfaces that bind consecutive dimers to one another was maintained, and only small rearrangements of the local contact network were observed.
evidence: This is based on analysis of MD simulation trajectories.

claim: Archaeasomes retain protein-protein contacts while allowing for significant molecular motion.
source: Together, these data show that archaeasomes retain protein-protein contacts while still allowing for significant molecular motion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MD simulation data showing maintained four-helix bundle interfaces despite large-scale dynamics.

claim: L1-L1 interactions drastically reduced the population of the accessible state in Arc120 and Arc180 simulations.
source: Simulations of Arc120 and Arc180 systems showed that L1-L1 interactions drastically reduced the population of the accessible state.
evidence: This is based on comparison of RMSD, RMSF, and DNA separation measurements between Arc90 (no L1-L1 interactions) and Arc120/Arc180 (with L1-L1 interactions).

claim: Both the maximum observed RMSD and variance in the timeseries were dampened in Arc120 and Arc180 systems compared to Arc90.
source: Both the maximum observed RMSD and variance in the timeseries were dampened in these systems (Figure 2A,B), and RMSF calculations showed that DNA bound to the terminal dimers were less dynamic than in Arc90 trajectories (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RMSD and RMSF analysis of MD simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Arc120-G17D system experienced increased dynamics relative to the wild-type Arc120 trajectories.
source: While the Arc120-G17D system has the proper number of dimers to form L1-L1 stacking interactions, the G17D mutation was designed to disfavor interactions, and this system experienced increased dynamics relative to the wild-type Arc120 trajectories.
evidence: This is based on RMSD, RMSF, and DNA separation measurements comparing Arc120-G17D to wild-type Arc120.

claim: The G17D mutation increased the solvent-accessible surface area by over 1,000 Å² compared to wild-type Arc120.
source: This also increased the solvent-accessible surface area by over 1,000 Å2 (57,316 ± 34 Å2 vs 58,422 ± 73 Å2, p-value<0.001; Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on solvent-accessible surface area calculations from MD simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The four-helix bundle interactions of consecutive dimers were maintained in Arc120-G17D systems despite the increase in DNA separation and surface accessibility.
source: Similar to the Arc90 system, the four-helix bundle interactions of consecutive dimers were maintained in these systems, despite the increase in DNA separation and surface accessibility.
evidence: This is based on analysis of MD simulation trajectories.

claim: Histone-DNA interactions were largely unchanged by the dynamics observed in simulations.
source: Histone-DNA interactions were largely unchanged by these dynamics.
evidence: This is based on MM-GBSA calculations of DNA binding energies from MD simulations.

claim: Raw MM-GBSA values suggest that DNA-binding strength increases as additional dimers are added to an archaeasome stack.
source: In agreement with previous computational studies (Rojec et al., 2019), raw MM-GBSA values suggest that DNA-binding strength increases as additional dimers are added to an archaeasome stack (ΔGArc90 < ΔGArc120 < ΔGArc180).
evidence: This is based on MM-GBSA calculations from MD simulations and is consistent with previous computational studies.

claim: When MM-GBSA values were normalized to the number of dimers in each system, there was no net change in DNA binding ability as a function of archaeasome size.
source: When MM-GBSA values were normalized to the number of dimers in each system, there was no net change in DNA binding ability as a function of archaeosome size.
evidence: This is based on normalized MM-GBSA calculations from MD simulations shown in Table 1.

claim: The G17D point mutation slightly reduced the dimer-DNA interaction strength, but this difference was not statistically significant when compared to the wild-type Arc120 system.
source: Additionally, the G17D point mutation slightly reduced the dimer-DNA interaction strength, but this difference was not statistically significant when compared to the wild-type Arc120 system (p-value of 0.157).
evidence: This is based on MM-GBSA calculations and statistical analysis from MD simulations.

claim: Archaeasomes can sample open and accessible conformations without histone dissociation.
source: These data, in conjunction with maintained four-helix bundle interactions, show that archaeasomes can sample open and accessible conformations without histone dissociation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MD simulation data showing maintained histone-histone and histone-DNA interactions despite increased accessibility.

claim: The loss of the 30 base pair ladder pattern in MNase digestion of chromatin from cells carrying the G17D mutation may be due to increased archaeasome dynamics rather than frequent histone dissociation.
source: Thus, the loss of the 30 base pair ladder pattern in MNase digestion of chromatin isolated from cells carrying the G17D mutation as their only source of histones may be due to increased archaeasome dynamics (Figure 3), rather than frequent histone dissociation (Mattiroli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the MD simulation data and comparison with previous experimental results.

claim: Full complex saturation of Arc207 occurs when DNA and histones are mixed at the stoichiometric limit of ~30 bp per dimer.
source: Gel shift assays showed that full complex saturation occurs when DNA and histones are mixed at the previously reported stoichiometric limit (~30 bp per dimer; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Mattiroli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on gel shift assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Arc207 complex sediments homogeneously at ~10.6 s.
source: SV-AUC traces show that the Arc207 complex sediments homogeneously at ~10.6 s (Figure 4, circles), and the Nuc147 control sediments more rapidly than the Arc207 system at ~11.2 s (Figure 4, squares).
evidence: This is based on SV-AUC data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The Nuc147 control sediments at ~11.2 s, more rapidly than the Arc207 system.
source: SV-AUC traces show that the Arc207 complex sediments homogeneously at ~10.6 s (Figure 4, circles), and the Nuc147 control sediments more rapidly than the Arc207 system at ~11.2 s (Figure 4, squares).
evidence: This is based on SV-AUC data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The Arc207 complex is fully saturated with histones and has a total mass consistent with seven histone dimers assembled on 207 bp of DNA.
source: Nevertheless, these data show that the Arc207 complex is fully saturated with histones, that the total mass is consistent with seven histone dimers assembled on 207 bp of DNA, and that its mass is greater than that of Nuc147.
evidence: This is based on GA-MC analysis of SV-AUC data shown in Table 2.

claim: The Arc207 system is more anisotropic than Nuc147, as confirmed by frictional ratios (f/fo) of 1.94 and 1.55 for Arc207 and Nuc147, respectively.
source: This suggests that the Arc207 system is more anisotropic than Nuc147 in order to satisfy the decrease in sedimentation rate, which is confirmed by the frictional ratios (f/fo) estimated from GA-MC calculations (1.94 and 1.55 for Arc207 and Nuc147, respectively).
evidence: This is based on GA-MC analysis of SV-AUC data shown in Table 2.

claim: The Arc207 complex is more compact than free DNA but not as compact as the eukaryotic nucleosome.
source: For reference, the f/fo value of free 207 DNA is 3.14 so the Arc207 complex is more compact than free DNA but not as compact as the eukaryotic nucleosome.
evidence: This is based on comparison of frictional ratios from SV-AUC data.

claim: CryoEM data shows that the Arc207 system is open, exhibiting nucleosome-like particle dimensions with increased spacing between neighboring DNA gyres.
source: CryoEM data shows that the Arc207 system is indeed open, as it exhibits nucleosome-like particle dimensions with increased spacing between neighboring DNA gyres (Figure 4B), in agreement with SV-AUC data.
evidence: This is based on cryoEM micrographs and 2D classifications shown in Figure 4.

claim: Arc207 samples exhibit an increase in sedimentation rate with increased Mg2+ concentration from 0 to 5 mM, with no additional increase between 5 and 10 mM MgCl2.
source: Arc207 samples exhibit an increase in sedimentation rate with increased Mg2+ concentration from 0 to 5 mM, with no additional increase between 5 and 10 mM MgCl2 (Figure 5A, top).
evidence: This is based on SV-AUC data at varying Mg2+ concentrations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The nucleosome system shows little to no change in sedimentation from 0 to 2 mM MgCl2 and starts to self-associate (aggregate) at concentrations above 2 mM Mg2+.
source: In comparison, the nucleosome system shows little to no change in sedimentation from 0 to 2 mM MgCl2 (Figure 5A, bottom), and start to self-associate (aggregate) at concentrations above 2 mM Mg2+.
evidence: This is based on SV-AUC data at varying Mg2+ concentrations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Unlike eukaryotic chromatin, divalent cations compact archaeasomes without promoting fiber-fiber association.
source: This shows that, unlike eukaryotic chromatin, divalent cations compact archaeasomes without promoting fiber-fiber association.
evidence: This is based on comparison of SV-AUC data for Arc207 and Nuc147 at varying Mg2+ concentrations.

claim: Estimates of Mg2+ concentration within T. kodakarensis cells have been quoted at ~120 mM.
source: Interestingly, estimates of Mg2+ concentration within T. kodakarensis cells have been quoted at ~120 mM (Nagata et al., 2017), much higher than measurements of Mg2+ in mammalian nuclei (16–18 mM) (Romani, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nagata et al., 2017 and Romani, 2013.

claim: Measurements of Mg2+ in mammalian nuclei are 16–18 mM.
source: Interestingly, estimates of Mg2+ concentration within T. kodakarensis cells have been quoted at ~120 mM (Nagata et al., 2017), much higher than measurements of Mg2+ in mammalian nuclei (16–18 mM) (Romani, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Romani, 2013.

claim: Per dimer, archaeal histones provide weaker electrostatic screening of DNA than eukaryotic histones, due to their relatively lower isoelectric points (pI of ~8 vs ~11).
source: Per dimer, archaeal histones provide weaker electrostatic screening of DNA than eukaryotic histones, due to their relatively lower isoelectric points (pI of ~8 vs~11), and the greater overall negative charge of archaeasomes may encourage rapid sequestering of any free Mg2+ ions in the cell.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of histone properties and inference about electrostatic interactions.

claim: Two different populations of Arc207 were identified: Class I, which has the classical 'nucleosome-like' fold, and Class II, in which two perpendicular DNA wrappings are clearly observed.
source: The two-dimensional classification of this dataset identify two different populations of Arc207: Class I, which upon first inspection has the classical 'nucleosome-like' fold (Figure 6B), and Class II, in which two perpendicular DNA wrappings are clearly observed (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on 2D classification of cryoEM data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Refinement of Class I and Class II particles yielded maps at 9.5 Å and 11.5 Å resolution, respectively.
source: Refinement of these densities yielded maps at 9.5 Å and 11.5 Å resolution for Class I and Class II, respectively (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is based on 3D refinement of cryoEM data shown in Figure 6D and 6E.

claim: The Class II density describes only 150 base pairs of DNA and five histone dimers, even though Arc207 (207 base pairs of DNA bound to seven histone dimers) were deposited on the grid.
source: Even though Arc207 (207 base pairs of DNA bound to seven histone dimers) were deposited on the grid, refined density of state Class II describes only 150 base pairs of DNA and five histone dimers (Video 7).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the Class II cryoEM density shown in Video 7.

claim: MD simulations describe with high fidelity a compact archaeasome composed of five histone dimers wrapping ~150 bp of DNA, as shown by a correlation coefficient of 0.85 between simulated and empirical density.
source: We simulated density at 8 Å resolution for the MD-derived structure, which yields a correlation coefficient of 0.85 with the empirical map. This shows that our MD simulations describe with high fidelity a compact archaeasome composed of five histone dimers wrapping ~150 bp of DNA.
evidence: This is based on comparison of simulated density from MD structures with the empirical cryoEM map.

claim: The Class I density has sufficient volume to be fit with the full 207 base pair DNA and seven histone dimers.
source: The density for Class II has sufficient volume to be fit with the full 207 base pair DNA and seven histone dimers (Video 8).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the Class I cryoEM density shown in Video 8.

claim: In the Class I structure, the larger portion of the volume is best described by four histone dimers binding ~120 base pairs of DNA in a nucleosome-like structure, and the smaller portion can be fit with three histone dimers binding ~90 base pairs.
source: The larger portion of the volume is best described by four histone dimers binding ~120 base pairs of DNA in a nucleosome-like structure, and the smaller portion can be fit with three histone dimers binding ~90 base pairs.
evidence: This is based on rigid-body docking of structural models into the Class I cryoEM density.

claim: In the Class I structure, the wrapping pathways of the subunits result in the two faces being arranged at a near 90° angle.
source: While the connecting density suggests only moderate bends in the helical axis, the wrapping pathways of the subunits result in the two faces being arranged at a near 90° angle.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the Class I cryoEM density and fitted models.

claim: The connecting DNA segment between Arc120 and Arc90 subunits in the Class I structure is reconcilable with B-form DNA parameters.
source: Structural models were generated by rigid-body docking separate Arc120 and Arc90 subunits into the associated density, and the connecting DNA was energy minimized and subjected to a short MD simulation to confirm that the connecting DNA segment is reconcilable with B-form DNA parameters (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on energy minimization and MD simulation of the connecting DNA shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the fully resolved Arc207 model with the Arc90 'lid' bending ~90° from the Arc120 'core', the calculated frictional ratio is 1.53, in close agreement with the 1.55 value extracted from experimental SV-AUC traces.
source: For the fully resolved Arc207 model, with the Arc90 'lid' bending ~90o from the Arc120 'core', we calculate a frictional ratio of 1.53, in close agreement with the 1.55 value extracted from the experimental traces.
evidence: This is based on hydrodynamic calculations using the SoMo plugin and comparison with experimental SV-AUC data.

claim: Models with continuous wrapping and no deflections in the DNA pathway yield a frictional coefficient of 1.36.
source: In contrast, models with continuous wrapping and no deflections in the DNA pathway (as observed in the crystal structure, but not populated significantly in the cryo EM images) yield a frictional coefficient of 1.36.
evidence: This is based on hydrodynamic calculations using the SoMo plugin for alternative structural models.

claim: Archaeasomes on an extended DNA fragment can be viewed as a distribution of archaeasome subunits that can open to a ~90° angle.
source: These data together show that archaeasomes on an extended DNA fragment can be viewed as a distribution of archaeasome subunits that can open to a ~90o angle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined cryoEM, SV-AUC, and hydrodynamic modeling data.

claim: Archaeasomes are metastable and extended in the absence of divalent cations.
source: Our cryoEM structures show that archaeosomes are metastable and extended in the absence of divalent cations.
evidence: This is based on cryoEM data collected in the absence of Mg2+.

claim: Even in the presence of 5 mM Mg2+, archaeasomes exhibit at least two configurations.
source: Even in the presence of 5 mM Mg2+, archaeasomes exhibit at least two configurations.
evidence: This is based on cryoEM data showing two distinct classes of particles in the presence of 5 mM Mg2+.

claim: Archaeasome structures contain a maximum of four to five histone dimers arranged in a continuous helical ramp, beyond which the helical histone ramp is disrupted at the four-helix bundle interface by an outward rotation of the remaining two to three histone dimers and attached DNA.
source: Indeed, our structures contain a maximum of four to five histone dimers arranged in a continuous helical ramp. Beyond that, the helical histone ramp is disrupted at the four-helix bundle interface by an outward rotation of the remaining two to three histone dimers and attached DNA.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryoEM structures.

claim: The arrangement of archaeasome subunits at ~90 degree angles may leave the major groove of the connecting DNA susceptible to nuclear factors, such as micrococcal nuclease or transcription factors.
source: This arrangement may leave the major groove of the connecting DNA susceptible to nuclear factors, such as micrococcal nuclease or transcription factors, and explains the ~30 bp MNase digestion ladder observed in native archaeal chromatin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and comparison with MNase digestion patterns.

claim: The arrangement of archaeasome subunits at ~90 degree angles explains the ~30 bp MNase digestion ladder observed in native archaeal chromatin.
source: This arrangement may leave the major groove of the connecting DNA susceptible to nuclear factors, such as micrococcal nuclease or transcription factors, and explains the ~30 bp MNase digestion ladder observed in native archaeal chromatin.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the structural findings to previous experimental observations.

claim: Models constructed from repeats of the Arc90 conformation agree with particle conformations extracted from SV-AUC hydrodynamic parameters and direct images from cryoEM data gathered in the absence of Mg2+.
source: Models constructed from repeats of this conformation agree with particle conformations extracted from SV-AUC hydrodynamic parameters, as well as direct images and two-dimensional class averages from cryoEM data gathered in the absence of Mg2+.
evidence: This is based on comparison of MD simulation models with SV-AUC and cryoEM data.

claim: Arc120 and Arc180 simulations may have been artificially biased for the closed configuration because the starting structures had intact L1-L1 interactions.
source: However, these simulations may have been artificially biased for the closed configuration, because the starting structures had intact L1-L1 interactions.
evidence: This is speculation about potential limitations of the MD simulations.

claim: Separation of L1-L1 contacts may require more than several hundred nanoseconds of computational sampling.
source: Separation of these contacts may require more than several hundred nanoseconds of computational sampling, and simulations of the Arc120-G17D system indeed show appreciable separation between DNA turns by weakening this interface while maintaining four-helix bundle interactions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the timescales observed in the simulations.

claim: Substituting major type histones in Methanosphaera stadtmanae with a 'capstone' paralog disrupts the tetramer interface and separates histone dimers on a continuous DNA fragment, thereby limiting archaeasome size.
source: In a recent study by Stevens et al., 2020, molecular dynamics trajectories showed that substituting major type histones in Methanosphaera stadtmanae with a 'capstone' paralog, a histone variant with sequence modifications at the four-helix bundle, disrupts the tetramer interface and separates histone dimers on a continuous DNA fragment, thereby limiting archaeasome size.
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Stevens et al., 2020.

claim: Destabilizing the four-helix bundle interface may yield a subtle increase in DNA accessibility through increased exposure of the major groove without the need to fully displace the archaeasome subunit.
source: In the context of the capstone model, our EM-derived structures suggest that destabilizing the four-helix bundle interface may yield a subtle increase in DNA accessibility through increased exposure of the major groove, and without the need to fully displace the archaeasome subunit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and the capstone model.

claim: Arc207 assemblies exhibit no signs of self-association upon the addition of up to 10 mM MgCl2, unlike eukaryotic nucleosomes and nucleosome arrays.
source: Our SV-AUC traces show that Arc207 assemblies exhibit no signs of self-association upon the addition of up to 10 mM MgCl2, unlike eukaryotic nucleosomes and nucleosome arrays, where this favors extensive inter-nucleosome and inter-array interactions and aggregation (Schwarz et al., 1996).
evidence: This is based on SV-AUC data and comparison with known behavior of eukaryotic nucleosomes.

claim: Divalent cations bias individual archaeasomes toward more compact states without promoting inter-archaeasome interactions.
source: Instead, these conditions bias individual archaeasomes toward more compact states without promoting inter-archaeasome interactions.
evidence: This is based on SV-AUC data showing compaction without aggregation.

claim: The ability of T. kodakarensis archaeasomes to compact but not aggregate as a result of elevated Mg2+ concentration may be a direct result of evolving in high-salt environments.
source: On the other hand, the ability of T. kodakarensis archaeasomes to compact but not aggregate as a result of elevated Mg2+ concentration may be a direct result of evolving in high-salt environments, as regulating between internal and external concentrations may have been more energetically demanding than simply adapting their chromatin structure.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary adaptation.

claim: Archaeal histones were successfully expressed in E. coli cells and were found to coat bacterial DNA.
source: Archaeal histones were successfully expressed in E. coli cells and were found to coat bacterial DNA (Rojec et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Rojec et al., 2019.

claim: Expression of archaeal histones in E. coli resulted in only minor perturbations of cell growth, despite E. coli lacking the evolutionary machinery to handle histones.
source: Surprisingly, this resulted in only minor perturbations of cell growth, despite E. coli lacking the evolutionary machinery to handle histones.
evidence: This is based on the citation to Rojec et al., 2019.

claim: In vitro assays have shown that transcription through archaeasomes is slowed but not altogether stopped.
source: Furthermore, in vitro assays have shown that transcription through archaeasomes is slowed but not altogether stopped (Xie and Reeve, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Xie and Reeve, 2004.

claim: In eukaryotes, navigation of polymerases through chromatin is assisted by histone chaperones and ATP-dependent remodeling factors.
source: In eukaryotes, navigation of polymerases through chromatin is assisted by histone chaperones and ATP-dependent remodeling factors (Hammond et al., 2017; Clapier et al., 2017; Markert and Luger, 2021), but no known homologs to these complexes have been identified as yet in archaea.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature on chromatin remodeling.

claim: No known homologs to histone chaperones and ATP-dependent remodeling factors have been identified as yet in archaea.
source: In eukaryotes, navigation of polymerases through chromatin is assisted by histone chaperones and ATP-dependent remodeling factors (Hammond et al., 2017; Clapier et al., 2017; Markert and Luger, 2021), but no known homologs to these complexes have been identified as yet in archaea.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In absence of remodelers, the inherent dynamics of archaeasome-based chromatin may allow limited access to chromatin by the sporadic appearance of near-zero linker DNA and Arc60 or Arc90 substates.
source: In absence of remodelers, the inherent dynamics of archaeasome-based chromatin may thereby allow limited access to chromatin by the sporadic (and possibly stochastic) appearance of near-zero linker DNA and Arc60 or Arc90 substates.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural and dynamic findings.

claim: The 'SMC-like' coalescin protein was recently identified in the histone-less Sulfolobus archaea.
source: On a related note, the 'SMC-like' coalescin proteins was recently identified in the histone-less Sulfolobus archaea (Takemata and Bell, 2021), and the access of these yet unidentified 'hidden agents' would similarly be tuned by the dynamics of the archaeasome.
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Takemata and Bell, 2021.

claim: HTkA histones from Thermococcus kodakarensis are very similar to HMfB histones (overall 59% identity, 81% similarity, with higher conservation in sequences involved in histone-histone and histone-DNA interactions).
source: We reconstituted archaeasomes on 207 base pairs of Widom 601 DNA (Arc207) with saturating amounts of recombinant HTkA histones from Thermococcus kodakarensis, which are very similar to HMfB histones (overall 59% identity, 81% similarity, with higher conservation in sequences involved in histone-histone and histone-DNA interactions) (Mattiroli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Mattiroli et al., 2017.

claim: Three independent simulations of each archaeasome system were conducted for 300 ns in the NPT ensemble.
source: After energy minimization, three independent simulations of each system were conducted according to the following protocol: simulations were heated from 10 K to 300 K over the course of 50 ps in the NVT ensemble with heavy atom restraints applied, system densities were equilibrated and positional restraints were slowly released over the course of 200 ps in the NPT ensemble (target pressure of 1 atm), and simulations were extended for 300 ns without positional restraints in the NPT ensemble.
evidence: This describes the MD simulation protocol used in the study.

claim: Reconstructed cryoEM volumes were deposited to the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMD-23403, EMD-23404).
source: Reconstructed volumes were deposited to the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMD-23403, EMD-23404).
evidence: This is a statement about data deposition.
